_description: Storage I/O latency thresholds (KCS-7132512). Source of truth for the Prometheus alert expressions in alerts/bsod-risk-prometheusrules.yaml and the guest-side alerts, bound by scripts/ci/validate-shared-thresholds.py.
_why:
H-5. The hypervisor alerts previously fired at an hourly MEAN of 30 seconds per read. IoTimeoutValue is breached by an INDIVIDUAL I/O exceeding the timeout, and what causes MEMORY_MANAGEMENT (0x1A) / KERNEL_DATA_INPAGE_ERROR (0x7A) is a TAIL event -- a p99 spike during a storage brownout or controller failover. A one-hour mean of 30 s/op requires essentially every I/O in that hour to take 30 seconds; a Windows guest in that state has been unusable for an hour and has already bugchecked. The alert therefore fired, if ever, strictly AFTER the event it existed to predict.

Worse, the framework's own Python analyzer flags the same physical quantity at 500ms (LATENCY_FAIL_THRESHOLD_MS) -- a ~60x sensitivity gap in which the LESS sensitive layer was the always-on, customer-facing one. An operator who deployed the alerts and never ran must-gather had effectively no storage-latency detection.
_units: seconds per I/O operation. Derived as rate(kubevirt_vmi_storage_read_times_seconds_total) / rate(kubevirt_vmi_storage_iops_read_total) and, since v0.26.0 (F-01), the same ratio over the WRITE counters; the alerts consume bsod:vmi_disk_latency:worst_1h, the per-disk max of the two. NOT milliseconds -- the Python analyzer's early-warning thresholds are in ms and are a different scale by design (see bsod_storage_checks.check_storage_io_latency). One threshold set covers both directions: the 60s VirtIO IoTimeoutValue these thresholds exist to predict is direction-agnostic, so there is no basis for grading a slow write differently from a slow read.
_sustained_warn_note: Aligns the always-on Prometheus layer with the analyzer's own 500ms FAIL. A sustained hourly mean at or above this is already deeply abnormal for enterprise virtualization storage and is predictive of the brownout conditions that produce tail spikes.
_sustained_critical_note: Sustained mean at or above 1 s/op indicates severe degradation. Supersedes the previous 30 s/op rule, which is subsumed (anything at 30 also exceeds 1).
_burst_note: Tail-latency approximation. KubeVirt exposes no _bucket histograms (see CLAUDE.md), so true percentiles are unavailable. max_over_time() of a short-window rate surfaces spikes that an hourly mean erases -- the closest available proxy for the p99 behaviour that actually triggers IoTimeoutValue.
_trend_note: 1h mean vs 24h baseline. Combined with sustained_warn_seconds so a low-but-rising VM is caught before it reaches the critical threshold.
_virtio_io_timeout_note: The value an individual I/O must exceed to trip the VirtIO storage timeout. Referenced in alert descriptions for context; it is NOT an alerting threshold on a mean (that was the H-5 defect).
_calibration_status:
PARTIAL (2026-07-29), AND READ-PATH ONLY. Measured on OCP 4.21.10 / CNV 4.21.13 against EXTERNAL ODF/Ceph RBD (ocs-external-storagecluster-ceph-rbd) with 15 concurrently running Windows VMs, sampled by scripts/cnv-storage-latency-calibrate.sh over a 24h window (5 active series, >0.5 read IOPS):
    p50 0.0040  p95 0.0299  p99 0.1406  max 0.1688 s/op
The 0.1688 peak was a SIMULTANEOUS 15-VM Windows boot storm (all VMIs 140m old at sample time) -- i.e. the heaviest I/O event this cluster produces -- and it sits 3.0x under the 0.5 s/op WARN threshold.

WHAT THIS ESTABLISHES: the shipped thresholds do NOT false-positive on a realistic enterprise backend under worst-case-normal load. That is why 0.5/1.0 were retained rather than adjusted.

WHAT IT DOES NOT ESTABLISH, and why this is still PARTIAL:
  0. ANY write-path behaviour. scripts/cnv-storage-latency-calibrate.sh sampled only kubevirt_vmi_storage_iops_read_total when these numbers were recorded, so every figure below -- including the 3.0x margin -- describes READS. The write-side distribution has never been measured, and on a replicated backend it is the direction more likely to degrade first (F-01). The calibration script samples both directions as of v0.26.0; re-run it and record the write figures before treating the margin as whole-path.
  1. Production p95. This is a test/workshop cluster capped at ~15-16 concurrent VMs with no sustained heavy workload. It cannot produce a representative production distribution, and synthesising one here would record an artefact, not a measurement.
  2. Whether the thresholds CATCH a real storage brownout. This cluster has never had one. Absence of an alert on a healthy cluster is not evidence the alert works -- those are different claims.
  3. Margin at scale. 3.0x is comfortable but not large; a fleet with 3-4x this I/O density could approach WARN during simultaneous boot. Re-run the calibration script before scaling up.

TO CLOSE THIS: run scripts/cnv-storage-latency-calibrate.sh --window 7d against a cluster carrying real production Windows I/O and record the result here. The ACM policy remains `inform` until then. Tracked as GitLab issue sbr-virt/pg-ocp-virt-bsod#2.

_calibration_observed.cluster: OCP 4.21.10 / CNV 4.21.13, external ODF Ceph RBD
_calibration_observed._direction_note: Explicitly recorded because the sampler was read-only when these figures were taken (F-01). A later run using the v0.26.0 script should carry direction_sampled: "read+write".

_write_path_note: F-01 (v0.25.0 peer review). Before v0.26.0 every threshold in this file was applied ONLY to the read path -- a repo-wide search for kubevirt_vmi_storage_write_times_seconds_total returned zero hits across the alerts, recording rules, ACM policy, dashboards and the calibration script -- while the offline Python analyzer already evaluated max(read_latency_ms, write_latency_ms). The always-on customer-facing layer was therefore blind to a degradation the Red Hat-only layer would have caught. This matters most on the replicated backends this framework targets: on ODF/Ceph RBD a read can be served by one OSD while a write must be acknowledged by every replica, so during recovery or an OSD flap write latency can rise by an order of magnitude while read latency stays nominal.
